# PDE Characteristics

**Characteristics** are special curves (or surfaces in higher dimensions) in
the domain of a [[partial-differential-equations|PDE]] along which information
travels and along which the PDE simplifies. They serve two purposes:

- For **first-order** PDEs they reduce the problem to a family of
  [[ordinary-differential-equations|ODEs]], which is the
  [[method-of-characteristics]].
- For **second-order** PDEs they determine the *type* of the equation (hyperbolic,
  parabolic or elliptic), and with it the qualitative behaviour of solutions.

The guiding picture is the [[transport-equation]] $u_t+cu_x=0$: the solution
is constant along the lines $x-ct=\text{const}$, so these lines carry the
information, and all that matters is to follow them back to the initial data.

# First-Order PDEs

## Characteristic Curves

Consider the quasilinear first-order PDE for $u(x,y)$
$$
a(x,y,u)\,u_x+b(x,y,u)\,u_y=c(x,y,u).
$$
The left-hand side is a derivative of $u$ in the direction $(a,b)$ (see
[[gradient#Directional Derivative|directional derivative]]), so the PDE only
involves the behaviour of $u$ along that direction field. Follow a curve
$(x(s),y(s))$ whose tangent is $(a,b)$ and set $U(s)=u(x(s),y(s))$. By the
[[chain-rule|chain rule]]
$$
\frac{dU}{ds}=u_x\frac{dx}{ds}+u_y\frac{dy}{ds}=au_x+bu_y=c.
$$

:::{.definition data-title="Characteristic Equations"}

The **characteristic equations** of the PDE above are the ODE system
$$
\frac{dx}{ds}=a(x,y,u),\qquad\frac{dy}{ds}=b(x,y,u),\qquad\frac{du}{ds}=c(x,y,u).
$$
Their solution curves $(x(s),y(s),u(s))$ are the **characteristic curves**, and
their projections $(x(s),y(s))$ to the $(x,y)$-plane are the **characteristics**
(or *base characteristics*).

:::

> *Note:* In the *linear* case $a,b$ do not depend on $u$, so the base
> characteristics can be found first from $dy/dx=b/a$ and the equation for $u$
> is then solved along them. In the *quasilinear* case the three equations are
> coupled and must be solved together.

## Examples

:::{.example data-title="Constant Coefficients"}

For $u_t+cu_x=0$: $\dot t=1$, $\dot x=c$, $\dot u=0$. The characteristics are
the lines $x-ct=x_0$ and $u$ is constant on each, so
$u=\varphi(x-ct)$ for any function $\varphi$.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Rotation"}

For $yu_x-xu_y=0$: $\dot x=y$, $\dot y=-x$, $\dot u=0$. Since
$\frac{d}{ds}(x^2+y^2)=2xy-2xy=0$, the characteristics are circles
$x^2+y^2=r^2$ about the origin and $u$ is constant on each circle. The general
solution is
$$
u(x,y)=\varphi(x^2+y^2),
$$
a radially symmetric function, as we expect since the operator
$y\partial_x-x\partial_y$ is the generator of rotations.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Burgers' Equation (Characteristics Cross)"}

For $u_t+uu_x=0$ the speed depends on $u$: $\dot t=1$, $\dot x=u$, $\dot u=0$.
So $u$ is constant on each characteristic, which are therefore *straight* lines
$$
x=x_0+u_0(x_0)\,t,
$$
with slope determined by the initial data, and the solution is
$u(t,x)=u_0(x_0)$ where $x_0$ solves this equation. Take $u_0(x)=-x$. Then
$x=x_0(1-t)$, so
$$
u(t,x)=-\frac{x}{1-t}.
$$
All characteristics meet at the origin at $t=1$, where the solution blows up.
Beyond that time the classical solution breaks down (a *shock* forms). For
$u_0$ with $u_0'<0$ somewhere the breaking time is $t^*=-1/\min u_0'$.

:::

## Data on a Curve
To determine a solution we prescribe $u$ on an initial curve
$\Gamma:(x_0(r),y_0(r))$, $u=u_0(r)$, and take the characteristic through each
point of $\Gamma$ as the starting point of the ODE system.

:::{.theorem data-title="Non-characteristic Condition"}

If $a,b,c$ are smooth and the data curve $\Gamma$ is **transversal** to the
characteristics,
$$
a\,y_0'(r)-b\,x_0'(r)\neq0,
$$
then there is a unique local solution through $\Gamma$. If $\Gamma$ is itself a
characteristic, then either no solution exists or infinitely many do.

:::

:::{.proof}

The map $(r,s)\mapsto(x(r,s),y(r,s))$ obtained by solving the characteristic
equations from $\Gamma$ has Jacobian at $s=0$
$$
\det\begin{pmatrix}x_r&x_s\\y_r&y_s\end{pmatrix}=x_0'\,b-y_0'\,a\neq0,
$$
so by the inverse function theorem it is locally invertible, and
$u(x,y)=U(r(x,y),s(x,y))$ is a well-defined solution. If $\Gamma$ is
characteristic, $a y_0'-bx_0'=0$ and the map degenerates.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Data on a Characteristic"}

For $u_x+u_y=0$ the solutions are $u=\varphi(x-y)$ and the characteristics are
the lines $y=x+\text{const}$. If we prescribe $u(x,x)=g(x)$ on the
characteristic $y=x$ then $\varphi(0)=g(x)$ for all $x$, so there is no solution
unless $g$ is a constant and then there are infinitely many ($\varphi$ is
arbitrary away from $0$). Prescribing instead $u(x,0)=g(x)$ on the transversal
line $y=0$ gives the unique solution $u=g(x-y)$.

:::

# Second-Order PDEs

## Characteristic Curves
Consider the second-order PDE in two variables
$$
Au_{xx}+2Bu_{xy}+Cu_{yy}+(\text{lower order terms})=0,
$$
with coefficients $A,B,C$ functions of $(x,y)$. Seek new coordinates
$\xi=\xi(x,y)$ for which $u_{\xi\xi}$ does not appear. Substituting
$u(x,y)=v(\xi(x,y),\eta(x,y))$, the coefficient of $v_{\xi\xi}$ is
$$
A\xi_x^2+2B\xi_x\xi_y+C\xi_y^2,
$$
so we need $\xi$ to satisfy the first-order PDE $A\xi_x^2+2B\xi_x\xi_y+C\xi_y^2=0$.
Level sets $\xi=\text{const}$ are curves $y=y(x)$ with slope
$dy/dx=-\xi_x/\xi_y$, and substituting $\xi_x/\xi_y=-dy/dx$ gives:

:::{.definition data-title="Characteristic Equation"}

The **characteristic curves** of $Au_{xx}+2Bu_{xy}+Cu_{yy}+\dots=0$ are the
curves $y(x)$ solving
$$
A\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2-2B\frac{dy}{dx}+C=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{B\pm\sqrt{B^2-AC}}{A}.
$$

:::

The number of real characteristic families is determined by the sign of the
**discriminant** $D=B^2-AC$.

## Classification

:::{.definition data-title="Hyperbolic, Parabolic and Elliptic"}

At a point the equation is

- **hyperbolic** if $B^2-AC>0$: two real families of characteristics,
- **parabolic** if $B^2-AC=0$: one real family,
- **elliptic** if $B^2-AC<0$: no real characteristics.

:::

Using the characteristics as coordinates reduces the equation to a
**canonical form**:

| Type | Characteristic coordinates | Canonical form | Model |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hyperbolic | $\xi,\eta$ the two families | $v_{\xi\eta}+\dots=0$ | [[wave-equation]] |
| Parabolic | $\eta$ the single family, $\xi$ any independent | $v_{\xi\xi}+\dots=0$ | [[heat-equation]] |
| Elliptic | $\xi\pm i\eta$ complex family | $v_{\xi\xi}+v_{\eta\eta}+\dots=0$ | [[laplace-equation]] |

:::{.example data-title="The Model Equations"}

- *Wave equation* $u_{tt}-c^2u_{xx}=0$. In the variables $(t,x)$ we have
  $A=1,B=0,C=-c^2$, so $D=c^2>0$ and $dx/dt=\pm c$: the characteristics are
  $x\pm ct=\text{const}$. Taking these as coordinates gives $u_{\xi\eta}=0$, as
  in d'Alembert's solution.
- *Heat equation* $u_t=ku_{xx}$. In $(x,t)$, $A=k$ and $B=C=0$ so $D=0$:
  parabolic, with the single family $dt/dx=0$, i.e. the lines $t=\text{const}$.
- *Laplace equation* $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$. $A=C=1,B=0$ so $D=-1<0$: elliptic,
  with no real characteristics ($dy/dx=\pm i$).

:::

:::{.example data-title="Reduction to Canonical Form"}

Consider $u_{xx}+2u_{xy}-3u_{yy}=0$. Here $A=1,B=1,C=-3$ and $D=4>0$, so it is
hyperbolic, with
$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=1\pm2\in\{3,-1\}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\xi=y-3x,\quad\eta=y+x.
$$
By the chain rule, $u_x=-3v_\xi+v_\eta$ and $u_y=v_\xi+v_\eta$, so
$$
\begin{aligned}
u_{xx}&=9v_{\xi\xi}-6v_{\xi\eta}+v_{\eta\eta},\\
u_{xy}&=-3v_{\xi\xi}-2v_{\xi\eta}+v_{\eta\eta},\\
u_{yy}&=v_{\xi\xi}+2v_{\xi\eta}+v_{\eta\eta},
\end{aligned}
$$
and the equation becomes $-16v_{\xi\eta}=0$. Hence $v=F(\xi)+G(\eta)$ and
$$
u(x,y)=F(y-3x)+G(y+x).
$$

:::

## Mixed Type
When the coefficients depend on position, the type can change from point to
point. The *Tricomi equation* $u_{xx}+xu_{yy}=0$ has $D=-x$, so it is
elliptic for $x>0$, parabolic on the line $x=0$ and hyperbolic for $x<0$. This
occurs for example in transonic flow, where the flow changes from subsonic
(elliptic) to supersonic (hyperbolic).

## Several Variables
For $\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}u_{x_ix_j}+\dots=0$ a surface $\{\phi=\text{const}\}$ is
**characteristic** if
$$
\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\,\phi_{x_i}\phi_{x_j}=0.
$$
For the wave equation this reads $\phi_t^2=c^2|\nabla\phi|^2$ (the *eikonal
equation*), whose solutions include the light cones $|x-x_0|=c(t-t_0)$. The type
is read from the signs of the eigenvalues of $(a_{ij})$: all the same sign is
elliptic, one sign differing from the rest is hyperbolic, and a zero eigenvalue
is parabolic.

# Interpretation

:::{.theorem data-title="Characteristics Carry Information"}

For a hyperbolic equation:

1. A discontinuity in the data (or in derivatives of the solution) is propagated
   *only* along the characteristics.
2. The solution at $(x_0,t_0)$ depends only on the data in the region bounded
   by the characteristics through that point (the *domain of dependence*), and
   influences only the region between the characteristics going forward (the
   *domain of influence*).

:::

| Type | Real characteristics | Information speed | Singularities | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hyperbolic | two families | finite | travel along characteristics | wave |
| Parabolic | one family | infinite | smoothed out instantly | heat |
| Elliptic | none | no propagation | solutions smooth in the interior | Laplace |

Elliptic equations have no characteristics, so no direction is special: the
solution at a point depends on the data on the whole boundary and is as smooth
as the coefficients allow. This is why elliptic problems are posed as boundary
value problems and hyperbolic and parabolic ones as initial value problems.

> *Note:* An initial curve being characteristic is exactly the degenerate case
> in which the Cauchy problem fails. For the wave equation the data
> $u,u_t$ on $t=0$ is fine, since $t=0$ is never a characteristic for $c<\infty$,
> but data on the light line $x=ct$ does not determine the solution.
